title: From Passive Listeners to Confident Readers: 4 Steps to Launch FASE Reading
author: Hanna Poorman
summary: Writing as a guest on Science of Reading Classroom, Hanna Poorman explains how she launched FASE, the shared oral reading routine from Teach Like a Champion, with students who could not be expected to be smooth from day one. She starts from the problem that popcorn reading breeds anxiety and inattention while teacher read-alouds model fluency but leave students passive. Her answer is a four-step scaffold: watch an exemplar video and surface student questions, practice choral reading with a familiar low-stakes text, have confident readers model the routine, and then call on everyone using the same easy text. Feedback is kept low stakes, for example by having a whole partner group reread a line rather than singling out one child. The routine takes several days, rereads and models to establish, but it becomes a daily practice that students look forward to. Her broader point is that student confidence is the foundation of a successful learning environment and that fluency routines need deliberate, gradual launch.
points: Popcorn reading and pure teacher read-alouds both fail to build fluency, which creates the need for a routine where every student engages with the text.
Launching FASE begins with students watching a real example and voicing their worries (getting stuck, not wanting to read aloud) before anyone is asked to read.
Using a familiar, low-stakes text such as The Three Little Pigs removes decoding surprises so students can focus on learning the routine itself.
Choral reading by partner groups and feedback given to the whole group let reluctant readers participate without exposure.
Having strong readers model the routine on day two shows classmates what success looks like before everyone is called on.
quotes: FASE is a shared oral reading system from Teach Like a Champion designed to encourage students to read fluently, expressively, independently, and joyfully.

I knew I wanted to use FASE in my classroom, but I also knew that my students wouldn’t pick it up right off the bat. There needed to be substantial scaffolding with gradual steps and consistent, explicit modeling before I could expect to see anything like the exemplar videos in my own classroom.
The most important part of this first step was to allow students to ask their questions:

Giving them this text allowed for no surprise multisyllabic words they might trip over. It also allowed them to feel a bit more confident going into the reading because they were already familiar with the story.
If I noticed the group didn’t read a line of dialogue with expression, I would point it out and make the entire group reread instead of an individual student.
This modeled for students what the routine looks like in our classroom.
My students didn’t just immediately do FASE effectively after I explained it to them. Instead, it required multiple days, reads, and models of this routine.

Student confidence is the foundation of a successful learning environment. Using an effective fluency routine where every student engages with the text creates a classroom culture of continuous growth without the pressure of being perfect.
